Cuckow
kŭk'ō
n. (an unclean fowl of the law; the Authorized Version's older spelling of cuckoo, though the bird intended is uncertain)
From the bird's call, Old French cucu; the 1611 spelling cuckow preserves the older English form. The Hebrew shachaph may name a gull or a shearwater rather than a cuckoo.

Definition · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

The word occurs twice, in the parallel lists of forbidden fowls: “And the owl, and the night hawk, and the cuckow, and the hawk after his kind” (Lev 11:16), and identically in the rehearsal of the law (Deu 14:15). Nothing else in Scripture is said about it, and the identification is not certain; the Hebrew word suggests a lean or slender bird and has been rendered gull or sea-mew as well as cuckoo. What the verse does establish is the shape of the whole catalogue: a run of night birds and hunters, each named, each with its family included by the phrase after his kind. Leviticus adds the wider rule about winged creatures: “All fowls that creep, going upon all four, shall be an abomination unto you” (Lev 11:20). And the chapter's purpose remains what it states at its close — a people sanctified because their God is holy (Lev 11:44).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines the cuckoo as a bird of the genus Cuculus, named from the sound of its note, and notorious for laying its eggs in the nests of other birds.

expand to see more

CUCKOO, n. [from the sound of its note.] A bird of the genus Cuculus.

The European cuckoo lays its eggs in the nests of other birds, to be hatched and reared by them.

The owl, and the night hawk, and the cuckow. Lev. xi.

CUCKOO-FLOWER, n. A plant, a species of Cardamine.

Key Scripture

Lev 11:16 — "And the owl, and the night hawk, and the cuckow, and the hawk after his kind,"

Deu 14:15 — "And the owl, and the night hawk, and the cuckow, and the hawk after his kind,"

Lev 11:20 — "All fowls that creep, going upon all four, shall be an abomination unto you."

Lev 11:44 — "For I am the LORD your God: ye shall therefore sanctify yourselves, and ye shall be holy; for I am holy: neither shall ye defile yourselves with any manner of creeping thing that creepeth upon the earth."

Modern Corruption

An archaic spelling and an uncertain bird are treated as evidence that the Authorized Version is unreliable, when the difficulty is lexical and is shared by every translation.

expand to see more

Cuckow is the 1611 spelling of a word we now write cuckoo, and the bird behind the Hebrew shachaph is genuinely uncertain — modern versions render it gull, sea gull, or long-eared owl, and none of them can be sure either. Two conclusions are drawn too quickly from this. The first is that the Authorized Version is obsolete because its English has aged; but an old spelling is not an error, and a reader who learns a hundred such words has gained access to the most influential English book ever printed rather than lost anything. The second is that uncertainty about a bird undermines confidence in Scripture; it does not, because the doctrine of the passage does not rest on the species. Every translation faces the same lexical gap, and honesty about it is a mark of careful work rather than a crack in the foundation.

It is worth saying plainly what this dictionary holds, since these lists are where the question usually surfaces. The Authorized Version is our working English text and its accuracy in the things that matter is not in doubt; where a Hebrew term for a bird or a stone cannot now be identified, that is a limit of our knowledge and not a defect in the word God gave. The standard the dictionary applies to itself is stricter than the one usually applied to translations: a quotation must match the version it claims, word for word. What ruins credibility is not an archaic spelling but a modern rendering printed under a label it does not belong to — and that is a fault of quotation, not of translation.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew shachaph (H7828), an unclean fowl rendered cuckow; from a root suggesting leanness; with tachmas (H8464), the night hawk, and netz (H5322), the hawk.

expand to see more

Hebrew shachaph (H7828) — rendered cuckow; occurring only in the two lists; Leviticus 11:16, Deuteronomy 14:15.

Hebrew tachmas (H8464) — the night hawk; named immediately before it; Leviticus 11:16.

Hebrew netz (H5322) — a hawk; the hawk after his kind; Leviticus 11:16, Job 39:26.

Hebrew bath yaanah — the owl, literally daughter of greed or of the wilderness; Leviticus 11:16.

Hebrew oph (H5775) — a fowl, anything that flies; the general category; Leviticus 11:13.

Usage

"“The owl, and the night hawk, and the cuckow” — a run of night birds, each named."

"“After his kind” — the family included with the bird."

"“All fowls that creep, going upon all four” — the wider rule of the chapter."
